To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
employees in partnership workplaces report higher union influence and greater levels of union commitment than employees in nonpartnership workplaces.
union members who work in partnership workplaces have a higher sense of union influence and a stronger commitment to their union than those who do not.

union members in partnership workplaces are: more satisfied with their union; more committed to the union; more likely to have joined their union in the last 5 years; and, more likely to recommend their union to others.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (1) Do unions working under partnership agreements benefit from the arrangements?
the impact of partnership on the attitudes and behaviours of employees.
the effects of partnership arrangements on unions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
unions benefit from working in partnership with employers.
unions working under partnership agreements do appear to benefit from their involvement in partnership, at least in Ireland.
the partnership experience has had positive effects for union influence and members’ commitment to unions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
partnership has a positive impact on union influence, and this in turn leads to greater union members commitment and loyalty to the union.
the Irish evidence suggests that unions can benefit from working in partnership with employers, at least in the short term.
the Irish evidence is consistent with the claim that partnership is a means by which unions may improve their influence and members commitment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
unions working under partnership have greater influence over the workplace than their counterparts in nonpartnership workplaces.
unions are more likely to be satisfied with the way they are treated by employers when they work in partnership with them.
unions are more likely to benefit from working in partnership with employers than they are to suffer as a consequence.
